title: Write It in Character
subtitle: Read the character + moment. Pick the line they'd really say.

drills.setup: Mara, a shy new kid who hides her nerves.
drills.prompt: Someone finally invites her to sit with them at lunch. Choose the line she'd really say.

options.text: “FINALLY! I thought you’d never ask me, this is the best day ever!”
options.why: That’s loud and gushing — a shy kid hiding her nerves wouldn’t burst out like this.

options.text: “Oh — um, sure. Thanks.” She slid onto the very edge of the seat.
“I already have a hundred friends, but okay, I guess.”
options.why: Boastful and cool is the opposite of a nervous new kid who’s glad to be included.

drills.teach: A shy character shows nerves through small, hesitant words + body language (the edge of the seat). The loud and the boastful lines don’t match “shy.”

drills.setup: Mr. Fen, a grumpy shopkeeper with a soft heart.
drills.prompt: A kid returns a coin he dropped earlier. Choose the line he'd really say.

options.text: “Hmph. Least somebody round here has manners.” He almost smiled.
“Oh thank you so much, you are my absolute hero forever!”
options.why: Gushing thanks breaks the grumpy voice — he wouldn’t fawn.

options.text: “Keep it. I don’t care about coins or anything else.”
options.why: Total indifference hides the soft heart — he does care, just gruffly.

drills.teach: Grumpy-but-kind = a gruff line with a hidden warm beat (“almost smiled”). Gushing thanks breaks the grumpy voice; total indifference hides the soft heart.

drills.setup: Kit, a brave younger sibling covering up fear.
drills.prompt: They hear a strange noise in the dark basement. Choose the line they'd really say.

options.text: “AAAH! I am NEVER going down there, you can’t make me!”
options.why: Full panic shows only fear — not the courage Kit is covering it with.

options.text: “I am not scared at all, not even a tiny little bit, nope.”
options.why: Over-insisting “not scared” tells us the feeling instead of showing it through action.

options.text: “It’s probably nothing.” Kit’s voice shook, but they took the first step down.

drills.teach: Brave-but-scared shows courage AND fear: a steady line undercut by a shaking voice, then action. Panicking or over-insisting “not scared” tells instead of shows.

drills.setup: Ana, a proud athlete who just lost a race.
drills.prompt: A teammate says “good try” at the finish line. Choose the line she'd really say.

options.text: “Thanks so much! Losing is totally fine and I feel great about it!”
options.why: Cheerful acceptance contradicts a proud competitor stinging from a loss.

options.text: “Yeah.” Ana stared at the track, jaw tight, and said nothing else.
“I meant to lose, I was just letting them win, obviously.”
options.why: A boastful excuse is telling, not showing — and it hides the real sting.

drills.teach: Pride after a loss shows through a clipped word + tense body (jaw tight). Cheerful acceptance and a boastful excuse both contradict a proud competitor stinging from a loss.

drills.prompt: They spot a strange machine humming in the corner. Choose the line they'd really say.

options.text: “What does THIS button do?” Dev was already reaching for it.
“A machine. Boring. Let’s go.” Dev walked straight past.
options.why: Indifference is the opposite of a curious inventor — Dev wouldn’t walk past a mystery.

options.text: “I hate machines and I never want to know how anything works.”
options.why: “Never want to know” contradicts curiosity itself.

drills.teach: Curiosity shows in the eager question + the hand already reaching. Indifference and “never want to know” are the opposite of a curious inventor.

drills.setup: Sam, a fiercely loyal best friend.
drills.prompt: Other kids start teasing Sam’s friend. Choose the line Sam would really say.

options.text: “Ha, good one!” Sam laughed along with the teasing.
options.why: Joining the teasing is exactly what a loyal friend would NOT do.

options.text: “Not my problem.” Sam looked away and kept walking.
options.why: Walking away abandons the friend — the opposite of fierce loyalty.

options.text: Sam stepped in front of them. “You want to say that again? To me?”

drills.teach: Loyalty shows in the action of stepping in + standing up for the friend. Joining the teasing or walking away are exactly what a loyal friend would NOT do.

drills.setup: Rosa, an exhausted parent at the end of a long day.
drills.prompt: Her kid asks for one more bedtime story. Choose the line she'd really say.

options.text: “One more.” Rosa sank onto the bed, already fighting a yawn. “A short one.”
“No stories EVER again, I am done with stories forever!”
options.why: A harsh, absolute refusal misses the loving-but-exhausted feeling.

options.text: “Sure, I have unlimited energy and could read all night long!”
options.why: “Unlimited energy” contradicts an exhausted parent at the end of a long day.

drills.teach: Tired-but-loving shows through a small yes plus the yawn and sinking down. The harsh refusal and the “unlimited energy” both miss the exhausted-but-still-there feeling.

drills.setup: Theo, nervous before his first stage performance.
drills.prompt: The curtain is about to rise. Choose the line — or action — that fits Theo.

options.text: “I’ve never been nervous once in my entire life about anything.”
options.why: Denying all nerves tells the opposite of what a first-timer feels — and it isn’t shown.

options.text: Theo peeked through the curtain, swallowed hard, and whispered, “Okay. Okay.”
“I hope I forget every single line and ruin the whole show.”
options.why: Wishing to fail doesn’t fit a nervous performer who wants to do well.

drills.teach: Stage nerves show through the peek, the hard swallow, and the self-steadying whisper — feeling revealed by action. Denying all nerves or wishing to fail don’t fit a nervous first-timer.
